title: The Economy of Trust
text:
Trust is among the most fragile of social assets, yet it underpins nearly every form of cooperation. Its value lies not in its presence but in its reliability: a person who is trusted consistently is granted credibility that no single declaration could secure. Because trust accumulates slowly and collapses quickly, institutions often treat it as a form of capital to be protected.

Scepticism, by contrast, is frequently mistaken for cynicism, although the two differ in an important way. A sceptic withholds belief until evidence justifies it, whereas a cynic assumes bad faith in advance. Maintaining integrity in public life therefore depends less on demanding blind faith than on sustaining scrutiny that remains open to being persuaded.

questions.text: What does the author imply about institutions?
options: They guard trust carefully because it is hard to rebuild.
They rarely depend on trust at all.

questions.text: What does the passage suggest about maintaining integrity in public life?
options: It requires openness to being persuaded by evidence.
It requires complete faith in leaders.
It requires assuming that others are dishonest.

paragraph_translations: A confiança é um dos bens sociais mais frágeis, e ainda assim sustenta quase toda forma de cooperação. Seu valor não está na simples presença, mas na sua confiabilidade: quem é consistentemente confiável recebe uma credibilidade que nenhuma declaração isolada poderia garantir. Como a confiança se acumula devagar e desmorona depressa, as instituições costumam tratá-la como um capital que precisa ser protegido.

O ceticismo, em contraste, é frequentemente confundido com cinismo, embora os dois sejam diferentes de um modo importante. Um cético suspende a crença até que as evidências a justifiquem, enquanto um cínico presume má-fé de antemão. Manter a integridade na vida pública depende, portanto, menos de exigir fé cega do que de sustentar um escrutínio que continue aberto a ser convencido.
